title: “Just Ask” Is the #1 Career Skill (Pay, Promotions, Power)
guest: Mandy Ginsburg, former CEO of Match Group; board member at Uber, ThredUp, Universal Music Group, formerly JC Penney and Care.com; private equity operating partner
summary: Mandy Ginsburg, who ran Match Group as a roughly $20 billion company, explains why she stepped down after a tornado and a health scare, how being a board member differs from operating, and how she ran a pay-equity audit at Match after noticing talented women never asked for raises. The core message is 'just ask' (for pay, promotions, anything), plus advice on investing in relationships rather than networking, choosing between options and RSUs, and building a career as a package deal with a trusted partner.

ideas.idea: Online dating grew because people stopped meeting at bars, churches and college; the first big audience was divorced parents with busy careers.
ideas.detail: With a divorce rate over 50 percent, match.com's early-2000s audience was 'second time around' people with little kids; Tinder later brought in younger groups and the category proliferated.

ideas.idea: Even a highly analytical product company must remember the numbers are people whose hopes are up.
ideas.detail: When a marketer complained that daily metric standups never talked about people, Mandy agreed: if the site goes down, those are people who might not meet.

ideas.idea: Listen to your instincts about when to leave; people almost always stay too long, and the best time is when the business is going well and a successor is ready.
ideas.detail: After nearly 15 years, a 2019 tornado destroyed half her Dallas house the week before earnings and a doctor's office 'fired' her as a patient over an unanswered breast-implant recall; she resigned in early 2020 with zero transition because co-leader Shar Dubey took over, six weeks before COVID shut the world down and dating boomed.

ideas.idea: A long-tenured CEO should ask whether they are still the person who will disrupt the company for the next 2 to 7 years.
ideas.detail: Mandy worried 'old dog, old tricks' and wanted fresh thinking to keep Match self-disrupting, though she says she has a different view in retrospect. She had asked the board to make her and Shar co-CEOs and was refused, but ran it as a tag team anyway.

ideas.idea: Her biggest asset as CEO was a team-sports mindset: genuine curiosity about people, loving to see them succeed, and the underrated skill of building community anywhere.
ideas.detail: She played serious soccer at Berkeley and was never the best or fastest player; she says among any ten friends there is one who could be dropped anywhere in the world and have a community in 30 days, and she discovered she was that person only by doing it.

ideas.idea: A board member must be 'fingers out, nose in' rather than 'fingers in, nose in' like an operator.
ideas.detail: A smart board chair gave her the phrase; operators want to say 'just do what I say' but management only listens and hopefully takes advice. The exception is a crisis like JC Penney's bankruptcy and CEO search, where board work becomes very hands-on.

ideas.idea: Board seats come through relationships built over years, not through networking for its own sake.
ideas.detail: Her first board, Care.com, came from a founder she befriended at a conference; the ThredUp seat came because chairwoman Patricia Nakache served with her on Care.com and they kept catching up every four to six months.

ideas.idea: Boards recruit for a specific superpower; Mandy's is 15 years of digital consumer subscription, acquisition and retention experience.
ideas.detail: Dara Khosrowshahi recruited her to Uber's board because it lacked digital consumer subscription operators as Uber One grew; Universal Music Group wanted subscription expertise for its Spotify relationship despite her knowing nothing about music.

ideas.idea: Saying yes to too many interesting opportunities is a weakness; she planned a year of pasta in Florence and ended up on many boards instead.
ideas.detail: She never aspired to be a board member or even CEO, joined her first board purely to learn what a boardroom is like, and now uses boards to stay abreast of technology and AI.

ideas.idea: Give employees a choice between stock options and RSUs so they can manage their own risk tolerance.
ideas.detail: Options are higher risk and higher potential reward; RSUs feel more cash-like. Match offered the choice and Mandy has introduced it at other companies; most humans, given the choice, pick the less risky outcome.

ideas.idea: Executive compensation is as much psychology as best practice, and must be aligned to actual value creation.
ideas.detail: She has seen the people who drive the most impact underpaid and others make far more than they were worth; compensation is never perfect, so aim to get it mostly right and tied to shareholder return.

ideas.idea: Run a pay-equity audit because men pound the table and ask for money while many talented women never will.
ideas.detail: Inspired by Salesforce's audit 13-14 years ago; a brilliant, analytical Asian immigrant product marketer on her team would never ask, so Mandy and Shar deliberately paid on contribution within bands. She ran the audit twice because she did not believe the equity result; the one anomaly was accounting, where long-tenured women were paid less than newly hired men.

ideas.idea: Outside hires get paid more than loyal long-tenured employees, so compensation drifts out of whack unless leaders actively correct it.
ideas.detail: This was the mechanism behind the accounting-department gap at Match; Jean adds that she only asked for a raise once, when people she had hired several levels below her were paid more than she was.

ideas.idea: Just ask: even if you get a no, asking plants in your manager's head that it matters to you, and squeaky wheels do get paid more.
ideas.detail: Mandy's mother trained her to 'open up your mouth and ask' and often said no, so she is fine hearing it; she hates that squeaky wheels get paid more but says it is a fact. The worst case is rejection, so compare it to the best case.

ideas.idea: Asking is a muscle to train in every domain, and girls must be taught to speak up at puberty, exactly when they start to pull back.
ideas.detail: The hosts note it is especially hard if you did not grow up asking; it applies to promotions, relationships and family, not just pay.

ideas.idea: Saying a goal out loud or writing it down makes it real and helps it happen.
ideas.detail: Cherie has been doing The Artist's Way daily journaling and finds that written-down thoughts tend to happen; Mandy agrees that voicing an ask moves it from your brain into the physical world.

ideas.idea: The most reliable path to a public board is being a public CEO; otherwise target private boards that need a specific skill like HR, talent, or CFO/audit expertise.
ideas.detail: Mandy teaches a women-in-boards course at Wharton and always gets asked how she got her seats; she distinguishes public boards, which want prior public-company experience, from private boards heading toward IPO.

ideas.idea: Men on boards bond over golf and shared university boards; women should create their own rituals, like dinner the night before a strategy session.
ideas.detail: When she invited the women on Uber's board to dinner they said no one had ever asked; women skip relationship-building because they are caring for kids and parents and see it as inefficient, and she notes she never waits for a women's bathroom at board events.

ideas.idea: Invest in relationships with people you admire because they make you happy, not to network; those are the ones that bear fruit in boards, advising and investing.
ideas.detail: Write a list of the people from your first job onward you want to keep up with and ask what they will be doing in six months, a year, ten years; women are worse at this than men.

ideas.idea: Once you have earned it, sell yourself as a package deal with a partner you are better with than alone.
ideas.detail: Mandy and Shar Dubey joined private equity firms together as operating partners, telling firms 'you have to hire us together'; she says she would not have done this in her late 20s or 30s and had to slog it out first. The hosts relate it to choosing who they work with at their own company.

ideas.idea: Hire people who are unlike you: an instinctive, creative decision maker should surround herself with analytical ones.
ideas.detail: Team dynamic assessments at Match showed how few people were like her; in personal life she attracts contemplative introverts like her husband.

ideas.idea: Compete with yourself more than with others.
ideas.detail: Asked who she secretly competes with, Mandy answered herself, and says she knows it.
